name: Abstraction, Pure Virtual Functions, and Interface Design
subject: Object-Oriented Programming Systems

mcqs.question: What makes a class an "abstract class" in C++?
options: Declaring all member variables as private
Declaring at least one pure virtual function using "= 0"
Preceding the class keyword with the abstract modifier
mcqs.explanation: In C++, any class containing at least one pure virtual function (syntax: virtual returnType func() = 0;) is an abstract class and cannot be instantiated.

mcqs.question: What happens if a derived class fails to override a pure virtual function from its base class?
options: The program compiles but crashes with SIGSEGV at runtime
The derived class also becomes an abstract class and cannot be instantiated
The compiler silently generates a stub function returning 0
The compiler emits a warning and uses standard library defaults
mcqs.explanation: If a derived class does not override all pure virtual functions, it inherits them as pure virtual, rendering the derived class abstract as well.

mcqs.question: Why must every base class intended for polymorphic deletion have a virtual destructor?
options: C++ compilers reject base classes without virtual destructors
To prevent undefined behavior and ensure the derived class destructor executes when deleting via a base pointer
To ensure that constructors are called in reverse order
To allocate destructor code on the heap rather than stack
mcqs.explanation: Deleting a derived object through a pointer to a base class without a virtual destructor results in undefined behavior (usually derived destructor is skipped, leaking resources).
